card.title: Even a coin toss didn't change minds

panels.text: 1967. Edward Jones and Victor Harris had people read essays for and against Fidel Castro, then rate how pro-Castro each writer was.
When readers thought the writers freely chose their side, they rated the pro-Castro writers as more pro-Castro. That seems fair.
Then came the twist. Readers were told the writers' positions were decided by a coin toss. They still rated the pro-Castro writers as more favourable to Castro.
Readers could not properly see the pull of the situation. A decade later Lee Ross named this the fundamental attribution error: we favour a person's character over their circumstances.

probes.question: What decided the writers' positions in the twist version of the study?
True or false: readers stopped attributing sincere belief to writers once they learned it was a coin toss.

claims.claim: Subjects read essays for and against Fidel Castro and rated the writers' pro-Castro attitude
claims.quote: Subjects in an experiment read essays for and against Fidel Castro

claims.claim: 1967, Edward Jones and Victor Harris; Lee Ross named the error a decade later
claims.quote: The phrase was coined by Lee Ross 10 years after an experiment by Edward E. Jones and Victor Harris in 1967.

claims.claim: When writers freely chose, pro-Castro writers were rated more pro-Castro
claims.quote: they would normally rate the people who praised Castro as having a more positive attitude towards Castro

claims.claim: Told the position was decided by a coin toss, readers still rated pro-Castro writers as more favourable (probe 1)
claims.quote: when the subjects were told that the writers' positions were determined by a coin toss, they still rated writers who spoke in favor

claims.claim: Readers could not properly see the pull of the situation; kept attributing sincere belief (probe 2)
claims.quote: they could not refrain from attributing sincere belief to the writers

claims.claim: FAE: we favour a person's character over their circumstances
claims.quote: observers underemphasize situational and environmental factors for the behavior of an actor while overemphasizing dispositional or personality factors
